weekLabel: Week 7 · Meeting A · Spatial Data, Scale, and Maps

slides.title: Geometry needs a ruler before it means anything
slides.subtitle: Geometry vs. attributes, GeoDataFrame, CRS and EPSG codes, projected vs. geographic measurement, buffer, and spatial join
slides.teaching: Open by asking: if I tell you two points are '0.000098 apart,' do you know how far apart they are? Today answers that question.

slides.title: A map is only as trustworthy as its geometry and its CRS
slides.statement: Where something is, and what units that 'where' is measured in, are two separate facts you must both get right.
slides.supporting: Geopandas will happily compute an area or a distance in the wrong coordinate reference system without stopping you. It is your job to notice.
slides.teaching: Foreshadow the two demonstrations coming later this deck: a distance measurement and an area measurement, both wrong in a geographic CRS, both fixed by reprojecting.

outcomes.head: Distinguish
outcomes.body: Tell geometry (shape/location) apart from attributes (everything else) in one spatial table.

outcomes.head: Choose
outcomes.body: Pick point, line, or polygon geometry for a given architectural question.

outcomes.head: Build
outcomes.body: Read or build a GeoDataFrame and identify its CRS by EPSG code.

outcomes.head: Reproject
outcomes.body: Explain why area and length calculations require a projected CRS, then use buffer and spatial join correctly.

slides.teaching: Preview that all four skills feed directly into Meeting B's studio and into Project 1 Part IV's map option -- one of two evidence-extension choices (map or Week 6's animation), not an unconditional requirement.

items: Geometry vs. attributes: two kinds of information, one table
Point, line, polygon: choosing the right geometry
Why projection matters: buffer and spatial join
slides.teaching: Tell students the whole arc builds toward one static map they will produce themselves on Wednesday.

slides.title: Geometry vs. attributes, defined

left.head: Geometry
left.body: The shape and location of a feature: a point, line, or polygon, stored in one special column (usually called geometry). Geometry answers 'where.'

right.head: Attributes
right.body: Every other column: room_type, zone, energy_kwh_m2_yr, and so on - ordinary pandas data describing 'what' about that location. A spatial table is just a regular table with one geometry column added.

slides.teaching: Point at a plain room schedule from Week 4-6: every column there is an attribute. Nothing in it says where a room actually is in space - that is exactly what today adds.

slides.title: A plain pandas table has no geometry column yet
slides.code:
import pandas as pd

plain = pd.DataFrame({
    'room_id': ['R101', 'R104'],
    'room_type': ['Lobby', 'Studio'],
    'x_m': [2.0, 2.0],
    'y_m': [4.0, 22.0],
})
print(plain.dtypes)
slides.output:
room_id          str
room_type        str
x_m          float64
y_m          float64
dtype: object
slides.explainBody: x_m and y_m are just two float columns here - pandas has no idea they describe a location. Every dtype is a familiar Week 4 type: str or float64. Nothing here is 'spatial' yet.
slides.teaching: Ask: could you compute a distance between these two rows right now? Not really - x_m and y_m are still just numbers, not a geometry Python understands as a shape.

slides.title: points_from_xy turns coordinates into real geometry
slides.code:
import geopandas as gpd

geom = gpd.points_from_xy(plain['x_m'], plain['y_m'])
sites = gpd.GeoDataFrame(plain, geometry=geom, crs='EPSG:32618')
print(sites.dtypes)
slides.output:
room_id           str
room_type         str
x_m           float64
y_m           float64
geometry     geometry
dtype: object
slides.explainHead: One new column, one new dtype
slides.explainBody: gpd.points_from_xy(x, y) builds a Point geometry object per row from two plain columns. The result carries a geometry dtype - geopandas now understands these rows as locations, not just numbers. crs tells it which coordinate system those x_m/y_m numbers are already in.
slides.teaching: Point at the new geometry row in dtypes. This exact pattern - a plain table plus points_from_xy - is how you would turn any x/y attribute table into a spatial one.

slides.title: GeoDataFrame, defined
slides.definition: A pandas DataFrame with one extra column (geometry) holding shapely geometry objects, plus a coordinate reference system recording what those coordinates mean -- defined precisely a few slides from now. Everything you already know about DataFrames -- columns, dtypes, filtering, groupby, merge -- still works.

example.head: gpd.GeoDataFrame(plain, geometry=..., crs=...)
example.body: Build one from a plain DataFrame plus a geometry column and a crs argument, exactly as the previous slide just did -- or load one directly with gpd.read_file(). GeoPandas adds exactly two things on top of pandas: a geometry column and a CRS.

slides.note: GeoPandas is not a new library to learn from scratch -- it is pandas plus a geometry column and a CRS. Today is about using both correctly.
slides.teaching: Reassure students: this is not 'yet another library,' it is pandas plus two additions. Reduces the perceived load of Week 7.

slides.title: Point, line, and polygon answer different design questions
rows: a site marker, a sensor, a room centroid
an ordered sequence of connected points
a circulation path, a property line, a utility run
a closed boundary enclosing an area
a zone footprint, a building outline, a room outline
slides.callout: Choose the geometry type the design question actually needs - a distance question wants a line; an area question wants a polygon.
slides.teaching: Ask students to name one geometry type for their own Project 1 site before moving on - this previews Part IV's map option, one of two evidence-extension choices alongside Week 6's animation.

slides.title: Point, line, and polygon are shapely objects with real properties
slides.code:
from shapely.geometry import Point, LineString, Polygon

site_marker = Point(2.0, 4.0)
egress_path = LineString([(2,4), (2,22), (18,22)])
zone_footprint = Polygon([(0,0), (24,0), (24,10), (0,10)])
print(site_marker.geom_type, site_marker)
print(egress_path.geom_type, 'length:', egress_path.length)
print(zone_footprint.geom_type, 'area:', zone_footprint.area)
slides.output:
Point POINT (2 4)
LineString length: 34.0
Polygon area: 240.0
slides.explainBody: These three literals use plain x, y numbers already understood to be meters (like Radley Hall's x_m/y_m columns), so .length and .area return sensible values right away - 34.0 m and 240.0 m2. The next slides show what happens when the coordinates are degrees of latitude/longitude instead.
slides.teaching: Confirm 240.0 m2 by hand: a 24 m x 10 m rectangle. Keep this number in mind - it reappears as Meeting B's known ground truth for the Radley Hall zone footprints.

slides.title: CRS, defined
slides.definition: A Coordinate Reference System states what a pair of numbers (x, y or lon, lat) actually means: which surface, which units, and which origin. Without a CRS, coordinates are just numbers -- geopandas cannot tell you if they are meters, degrees, or feet.

example.head: zones.crs
example.body: Printing a GeoDataFrame's .crs attribute reports the CRS geopandas currently has on record for it -- for example EPSG:4326 or EPSG:32618. Two GeoDataFrames must share a CRS before you can safely compare or join their geometries.

slides.note: A CRS is not a unit label typed into a column name -- it lives on the GeoDataFrame itself (gdf.crs), separate from any column, and travels with the geometry through most operations.
slides.teaching: Write both codes on the board - students will see exactly these two all studio long.

slides.title: EPSG code, defined
slides.definition: A short numeric ID for one specific, standardized CRS, maintained by a public registry. Two codes recur constantly in this course: EPSG:4326 (geographic, degrees of latitude/longitude, the GPS standard) and EPSG:32618 (UTM zone 18N, meters, the correct projected choice for Syracuse, NY).

example.head: crs='EPSG:32618'
example.body: Pass the EPSG code as a crs= argument when building a GeoDataFrame, or to set_crs()/to_crs() later -- always write it as the string 'EPSG:' followed by the number.

slides.note: EPSG:4326 is for storage and sharing - what GPS gives you. EPSG:32618 is for measuring - what you compute area, length, and distance with. The two are not interchangeable.
slides.teaching: Students will see exactly these two codes all studio long - 4326 for 'what GPS gives you,' 32618 for 'what you measure with.'

slides.title: gpd.read_file reports the CRS it found in the file
slides.code:
import geopandas as gpd

zones = gpd.read_file('zone_footprints.geojson')
print(zones)
print('CRS:', zones.crs)
slides.explainBody: This is the fictional Radley Hall zone-footprint file used in Meeting B - GeoJSON is a common text file format for storing geometry plus attributes together; gpd.read_file() reads it just like read_csv() reads a CSV. Its coordinates are longitude/latitude pairs - degrees, not meters - and geopandas correctly reports its CRS as EPSG:4326, the geographic default GPS coordinates arrive in.
slides.teaching: Point out the coordinate values themselves look like the Syracuse-area longitude/latitude students will recognize from the shared dataset README. Note North's row now has the higher-latitude coordinates - the file was corrected so the polygon plotted further north on the Northing axis is actually named North.

slides.title: A geometry built without a CRS argument has none
slides.code:
from shapely.geometry import Point
import geopandas as gpd

gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame({'room_id': ['R101']}, geometry=[Point(2.0, 4.0)])
print('crs before set_crs:', gdf.crs)

gdf = gdf.set_crs('EPSG:32618')
print('crs after set_crs:', gdf.crs)
slides.output:
crs before set_crs: None
crs after set_crs: EPSG:32618
slides.explainHead: None is a real, common bug source
slides.explainBody: If you forget crs= when building a GeoDataFrame, gdf.crs is simply None - geopandas has no idea what the coordinates mean. set_crs() states what CRS the coordinates ALREADY are in; it does not move or change any numbers.
slides.teaching: Contrast set_crs (label an existing coordinate system) with to_crs, coming next (actually convert the numbers to a different system). Students confuse these two constantly - name the difference explicitly now.

slides.title: Reprojection, defined
slides.definition: Reprojection converts a GeoDataFrame's coordinates from one CRS to another, recalculating every coordinate value so it still means the same real-world location under the new system. Unlike set_crs() (which only relabels and changes no numbers), to_crs() actually transforms the numbers.

example.head: gdf_utm = gdf.to_crs('EPSG:32618')
example.body: Every coordinate is recalculated from degrees of longitude/latitude into meters of UTM easting/northing. The location on the ground does not move -- only the numbers describing it change, and a NEW GeoDataFrame is returned.

slides.note: Calling to_crs() on a GeoDataFrame whose crs is None raises a ValueError: 'Cannot transform naive geometries. Please set a crs on the object first.' Set the CRS before you reproject.
slides.teaching: Contrast directly with the previous slide's set_crs - set_crs labels, to_crs transforms. This is the single most common Week 7 mix-up.

slides.title: Explode one reprojection call into its parts

parts.label: New GeoDataFrame
parts.body: to_crs() returns a NEW object -- it never modifies gdf in place.

parts.label: Original GeoDataFrame
parts.body: Still holds its current CRS and coordinates, untouched.

parts.label: Reprojection
parts.body: Recalculates every coordinate into the target CRS.

parts.label: Target CRS
parts.body: UTM zone 18N, meters -- the correct choice for Syracuse, NY.

slides.teaching: Walk left to right: a new name is created, the old GeoDataFrame is read but not changed, the method does the recalculation, and the string argument names the destination CRS.

slides.title: Degrees of latitude/longitude are not a ruler
slides.statement: A geographic CRS (like EPSG:4326) stores angles on a sphere. A projected CRS (like EPSG:32618) stores flat, linear meters.
slides.supporting: Area and length calculations need a consistent linear unit. Only a projected CRS gives you one - so reproject before you measure.
slides.teaching: This is the single most important idea in today's deck. Everything after this slide is proof.

slides.title: The same two zones, measured twice
slides.alt: Two panels of the same pair of zone polygons: the left in EPSG:4326 reporting an area of 2.65e-08 square degrees, the right in EPSG:32618 reporting 239.74 square meters against a known truth of 240.
slides.caption: Identical geometry, two coordinate systems. Only the right-hand number is an area.
slides.explainBody: Both panels ran .area on the same polygons. The left returned 2.65e-08 - real arithmetic in square degrees, a unit that does not describe ground area. The right returned 239.74 m2 against a known 240. The danger is that the wrong answer looks like an answer; nothing crashed.
slides.teaching: Ask what a student would conclude if they only ever saw the left panel's number and did not know what unit it was in. That is the whole case for stating your EPSG code.

slides.title: DEMO 1 - measure 8.0 m apart directly in EPSG:4326
slides.code:
import geopandas as gpd
from shapely.geometry import Point

# R101, R102 are 8.0 m apart on the ground
p1 = Point(-76.1350754186006, 43.03940661157025)
p2 = Point(-76.134977093003, 43.03940661157025)
gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame({'room_id': ['R101', 'R102']}, geometry=[p1, p2], crs='EPSG:4326')

d_geo = gdf.geometry.iloc[0].distance(gdf.geometry.iloc[1])
print(f'distance in EPSG:4326 (degrees): {d_geo:.6f}')
slides.explainBody: Two Radley Hall rooms known to be 8.0 m apart on the ground. Measured directly in EPSG:4326 (still degrees of longitude/latitude), .distance() returns 0.000098 -- a number of DEGREES, meaningless as a physical distance. The next slide reprojects and measures again.
slides.teaching: This is the shared, pre-verified Radley Hall CRS demonstration from data/README.md - use these exact numbers, do not recompute different ones. Let students sit with 0.000098 for a moment before revealing what it actually represents.

slides.title: DEMO 1, continued - reproject, then measure again
slides.code:
# gdf is still in EPSG:4326, from the previous slide
gdf_utm = gdf.to_crs('EPSG:32618')
d_utm = gdf_utm.geometry.iloc[0].distance(
    gdf_utm.geometry.iloc[1]
)
print(f'distance in EPSG:32618 (meters): {d_utm:.3f}')
slides.explainHead: 8.010 m -- within 1 cm of the truth
slides.explainBody: to_crs('EPSG:32618') reprojects gdf to UTM zone 18N (meters, the correct choice for Syracuse, NY); the same two points now measure 8.010 m -- within 0.010 m of the known 8.000 m ground truth. The small remainder is real projection distortion, not a mistake.
slides.teaching: Reveal this only after students have sat with how meaningless 0.000098 degrees is. Tie 8.010 m explicitly back to the known 8.000 m ground truth - the small gap is real distortion, not an error.

slides.title: Predict: what happens when you call .area in EPSG:4326?
slides.code:
import geopandas as gpd

zones = gpd.read_file('zone_footprints.geojson')
print(zones.crs)

areas = zones.geometry.area
print(areas)
slides.question: zones is still in EPSG:4326 (degrees). What happens next?
options: Warns, but still returns a number
slides.why: GeoPandas warns but still returns a number -- a tiny, meaningless square-degree value. It never reprojects for you automatically.
slides.teaching: Take a show of hands on every option before revealing. Many predict an error, since a value this wrong feels like it should stop the script - it does not.

slides.title: DEMO 2 - the same 240 m2 zone, measured two ways
slides.code:
import geopandas as gpd

zones = gpd.read_file('zone_footprints.geojson')
for zone, a in zip(zones['zone'], zones.geometry.area):
    print(f'{zone}: {a:.2e} sq deg')

zones_utm = zones.to_crs('EPSG:32618')
for zone, a in zip(zones_utm['zone'], zones_utm.geometry.area):
    print(f'{zone}: {a:.2f} m2')
slides.output:
North: 2.65e-08 sq deg
South: 2.65e-08 sq deg
North: 239.74 m2
South: 239.74 m2
slides.explainBody: Calling .area directly on EPSG:4326 geometry actually raises a UserWarning: 'Geometry is in a geographic CRS. Results from 'area' are likely incorrect.' (real, but printed to the console, not to the output panel here). Each Radley Hall zone is a 24 m x 10 m rectangle - 240 m2 by construction. Reprojected to EPSG:32618, both zones measure 239.74 m2: within about 0.1% of the known ground truth - a small, honest projection distortion, not an error.
slides.teaching: Read the real geopandas UserWarning text aloud once, unsuppressed, so students recognize it in their own console later. Tie 239.74 m2 forward explicitly - this is the exact number Meeting B's studio will reproduce.

slides.title: Same pattern, both times: reproject before you measure
slides.callout: Geographic-CRS numbers are not wrong arithmetic - they are the right math applied to the wrong unit.
slides.teaching: Have students say out loud, for each row, which column they would actually trust and why. The projected-CRS column is always within a fraction of a percent of ground truth; the geographic-CRS column is off by many orders of magnitude.

slides.title: Store globally, reproject locally, then measure

steps.label: EPSG:4326
steps.head: Store location
steps.body: Longitude and latitude describe angular position in degrees.

steps.label: SITE
steps.head: Choose projection
steps.body: Select a projected CRS whose valid zone contains the site.

steps.label: EPSG:32618
steps.head: Work in meters
steps.body: UTM 18N supplies linear units appropriate for the Syracuse example.

steps.label: MEASURE
steps.head: Check distance/area
steps.body: Compute only after reprojection and compare with a known scale.

slides.teaching: State the choice rule plainly: use a projection whose valid area contains the site. The fourth node keeps verification attached to the conversion.

slides.title: Predict, then verify: which number would you trust?
slides.prompt: Given a distance printed as 0.000041 in one CRS and 3.9 m in another, which is usable?
steps: Identify which CRS is geographic and which is projected.
State your prediction and why, before running anything.
Reproject the geographic version to EPSG:32618 and compare.
Write one sentence naming the correct CRS for a Syracuse, NY site.
slides.teaching: Expected answer: the projected (meters) value is usable; the geographic value is degrees, not a distance. Reinforces DEMO 1 with a fresh, unseen number.

slides.title: Buffer, defined
slides.definition: .buffer(distance) returns a new polygon: every point within distance of the original geometry. Call it on a point to get a disc-shaped review radius; on a line to get a corridor; on a polygon to get a setback or expansion.

example.head: site_marker.buffer(5.0)
example.body: On a GeoDataFrame already in EPSG:32618 (meters), buffer(5.0) returns a circular review zone with radius 5 m -- area near pi * 5^2 = 78.54 m2, verified on the next slide.

slides.note: distance is read in the GeoDataFrame's CURRENT CRS units. Buffer a point still in EPSG:4326 and distance means degrees, not meters -- reproject first, exactly like DEMO 1 and DEMO 2.
slides.teaching: Connect directly back to the two demos: buffer is just another operation that silently uses the wrong unit if you skip reprojecting.

slides.title: A 5 m buffer should have about pi times 5 squared area
slides.code:
import math
import geopandas as gpd
from shapely.geometry import Point

site_marker = gpd.GeoDataFrame({'id': [1]}, geometry=[Point(0.0, 0.0)], crs='EPSG:32618')
review_zone = site_marker.buffer(5.0)

print(review_zone.geom_type.iloc[0])
print(f'area: {review_zone.area.iloc[0]:.2f} m2')
print(f'pi * r^2 check: {math.pi * 5.0**2:.2f} m2')
slides.output:
Polygon
area: 78.41 m2
pi * r^2 check: 78.54 m2
slides.explainHead: A circle is really a many-sided polygon
slides.explainBody: buffer() returns a Polygon - internally, a many-sided approximation of a circle. Its area, 78.41 m2, sits just under the true circle area of 78.54 m2 (pi x 5^2) because the polygon approximation has a finite number of straight sides. This is a real, honest approximation, not a bug.
slides.teaching: Ask what would happen to that 78.41 vs 78.54 gap with a coarser or finer buffer resolution - not required to demo, just to build intuition that buffer is an approximation.

slides.title: Spatial join, defined
slides.definition: A spatial join matches rows between two GeoDataFrames by their spatial relationship -- for example, which point falls within which polygon -- instead of by a shared column value like an ordinary merge.

example.head: gpd.sjoin(markers, zones, how='left', predicate='within')
example.body: Attaches each zone's attributes to every marker point that falls within it. Both inputs must share the same CRS first, exactly as an ordinary merge needs a shared key column.

slides.note: how='left' keeps every row from markers, even a point inside no polygon (its new column becomes NaN). how='inner', the default if you omit how, would silently drop that row instead.
slides.teaching: Draw the parallel to Week 5 merge: a table merge matches values; a spatial join matches geometry. Both inputs must share a CRS.

slides.title: A spatial join uses location as the key

steps.label: LEFT
steps.head: Points
steps.body: Each marker keeps its identity and geometry.

steps.label: RIGHT
steps.head: Polygons
steps.body: Each zone carries attributes such as name or category.

steps.label: PREDICATE
steps.head: Test relation
steps.body: within, intersects, or contains defines what counts as a match.

steps.label: RESULT
steps.head: Attach attributes
steps.body: Matched zone information is added to each point row; unmatched rows remain visible.

slides.teaching: Walk through the four boxes using the upcoming three-point/two-polygon example before students see any code - LEFT is markers, RIGHT is zones, PREDICATE picks the rule, RESULT attaches attributes.

slides.title: Three site markers, two zone polygons: set up both layers
slides.code:
import geopandas as gpd
from shapely.geometry import Point, Polygon

markers = gpd.GeoDataFrame({'site_id': ['S1','S2','S3']}, geometry=[Point(5,5), Point(5,15), Point(30,30)], crs='EPSG:32618')
zone_a = Polygon([(0,0), (10,0), (10,10), (0,10)])
zone_b = Polygon([(0,10), (10,10), (10,20), (0,20)])
zones = gpd.GeoDataFrame({'zone_name': ['Zone A', 'Zone B']}, geometry=[zone_a, zone_b], crs='EPSG:32618')

print(markers.crs == zones.crs)
slides.explainHead: Same CRS, required before any join
slides.explainBody: S1 and S2 sit inside the two zone polygons; S3 sits well outside both. Both GeoDataFrames are built directly in EPSG:32618 (meters), so the join on the next slide can safely test within/intersects using real distances, not degrees. Confirming markers.crs == zones.crs is a habit worth keeping before every spatial join.
slides.teaching: Trace the three points and two boxes on the board now, before the predict slide asks students to reason about S3 -- this is the setup they need in hand.

slides.title: Predict: what happens to the point outside every zone?
slides.code:
joined = gpd.sjoin(
    markers, zones,
    how='left', predicate='within',
)
print(len(joined))
slides.question: S3 falls outside both zone polygons. What does len(joined) print?
slides.why: how='left' keeps every row, even S3. how='inner' (the default) would drop it and print 2. A join matches by location, not a shared column.
slides.teaching: Most predict 2, remembering merge's default inner-join behavior and not tracking the how='left' argument. Reveal, then run the real code on the next slide.

slides.title: Run the spatial join: who is where?
slides.code:
joined = gpd.sjoin(markers, zones, how='left', predicate='within')
print(joined[['site_id', 'zone_name']])
slides.output:
site_id zone_name
0      S1    Zone A
1      S2    Zone B
2      S3       NaN
slides.explainBody: S1 falls inside Zone A, S2 inside Zone B. S3 sits outside both polygons entirely, so how='left' keeps it in the result with zone_name as NaN - the point exists, it just is not inside any known zone. That NaN is real information, not a failure.
slides.teaching: Trace all three points against the two boxes on the board before revealing the printed table - this is exactly the kind of prediction step Meeting B's studio will ask for.

slides.title: Why this course does not spatial-join individual rooms

left.head: The pitfall
left.body: Radley Hall's room coordinates repeat: the same x_m, y_m location holds a room on floor 1, floor 2, and floor 3 (a real multi-story footprint). A point-in-polygon join on individual rooms would match several stacked rooms to the same zone at once - confusing, not wrong.

right.head: The fix Meeting B uses instead
right.body: Summarize first (Week 5's groupby, by zone), THEN join that one summary row per zone onto the zone polygon. One row per zone avoids the stacked-floor ambiguity completely, and is exactly the workflow needed if you choose the map for Project 1 Part IV -- one of two evidence-extension choices, alongside Week 6's animation.

slides.teaching: Be explicit that this is a modeling choice driven by the data's real structure, not a limitation of spatial joins in general - the toy S1/S2/S3 example above is exactly where a row-level join DOES make sense (one row, one place).

slides.title: Transfer the spatial join: which entrances fall inside shaded zones?
slides.prompt: Entrance points and shade polygons arrive in EPSG:4326; the team also needs a 5 m review radius around each entrance.
steps: Choose the point and polygon geometry roles and inspect both CRS values.
Reproject to EPSG:32618 before buffering or measuring distance.
Predict within versus intersects for an entrance exactly on a shade boundary.
Verify matched and unmatched points, then state the boundary rule used.
slides.teaching: The point-in-polygon join can be evaluated in a shared CRS, but any 5 m buffer or distance requires the projected CRS. A boundary point may fail within yet satisfy intersects; the team must state which predicate matches the decision. Require a visual or row-level check of unmatched entrances rather than trusting only the join count.

slides.title: The correct spatial workflow, every time

steps.label: LOAD
steps.head: Read the geometry
steps.body: gpd.read_file() and note its CRS immediately - do not assume.

steps.label: CHECK
steps.head: Confirm the CRS
steps.body: Geographic (degrees) or projected (meters)? Read the EPSG code.

steps.label: REPROJECT
steps.head: to_crs() before measuring
steps.body: Convert to a projected CRS (EPSG:32618 for Syracuse, NY) before any area, length, buffer, or distance.

steps.label: COMPUTE
steps.head: Measure or join
steps.body: Now .area, .length, .buffer(), and sjoin() all return trustworthy, checkable numbers.

slides.teaching: This four-step order is the single procedural takeaway students should be able to recite before Wednesday's studio.

slides.title: Spatial evidence now moves through open files and web APIs

steps.label: PACKAGE
steps.head: GeoParquet
steps.body: Geometry columns travel with declared encoding and CRS metadata in a columnar file.

steps.label: DISCOVER
steps.head: OGC API collections
steps.body: A client can discover available feature collections, extents, and capabilities.

steps.label: QUERY
steps.head: Request a bounded subset
steps.body: Filter by collection, spatial or attribute criteria, and only the fields needed.

steps.label: VERIFY
steps.head: Inspect before measuring
steps.body: Check schema, CRS, axis order, extent, missing geometry, and unmatched features.

slides.teaching: Optional horizon slide. GeoParquet and OGC APIs change delivery, not geometric truth. Rehearse the same refusal: do not measure distance or area until CRS and geometry validity are understood.

slides.title: Geometry plus a trustworthy CRS is what makes a map true
takeaways: Geometry (where) and attributes (what) are separate; a GeoDataFrame just adds a geometry column and a CRS to pandas.
EPSG:4326 (degrees) is for storage and sharing; EPSG:32618 (meters, UTM 18N) is for measuring at Syracuse, NY.
Reproject to a projected CRS before computing area, length, buffer, or distance - geographic-CRS numbers are real math applied to the wrong unit.
buffer() and sjoin() extend this same CRS discipline to proximity and location-based joins.
slides.teaching: Exit ticket: students write the EPSG code they will use for their own Project 1 site and one sentence justifying it.
